title: Patterns in the Dark

post.author: u/night_dispatch_vasilisa
post.title: I dispatch for a locksmith at night. Our app texted a woman locked out of her house the code to a key safe on a stranger's door across town. My notebook shows both texts.

blocks.text: I'm the night dispatcher at Cotterpin Locksmiths. People locked out ring me, and I send Teodric, our locksmith, out in the van. Each of those calls is a call-out. Many customers also pay us to fit a key safe by their door: a small locked box on the wall that holds a spare key and opens with a four-digit code. We keep the codes. When one of them rings at night, our app texts them their own code, and most are inside before Teodric arrives.
The app is a server: a program that waits for requests and answers them. Each call-out is one request, typed in by me or booked on our website.

Grisell writes the app in Node.js, a tool for running programs on a server. Node does one thing at a time, on one line of work called a thread. When a step has to wait for something slow, Node notes its place and starts on the next request.

Last month Grisell tidied the code. Each small piece of code that does one job, called a function, used to be handed its own call-out. Now one shared bundle of data, an object, holds the current job, and every request can reach it.
An object made only once and shared by the whole program is called a singleton.

Here is her code, in JavaScript, the programming language Node runs. The first lines make the shared object; each line inside dispatch is one step of a call-out, in order. The word *await* marks where a step waits while Node goes off to other work:

First it saves the call-out as the current job. Then it asks a map service to turn the address into a spot on the map. That service is called the geocoder. That takes about 300 ms, thousandths of a second. Then it texts the customer the key-safe code.

At 02:47:31.000 I typed a call-out for Ms Tremellen, locked out at 6 Bellfounder Row. Her code is 3158. At 02:47:31.200 another came in from the website: Mr Dunwiddie, 14 Haverick Close, across town. His code is 9026.

The app prints every text it sends into a job log I keep in a binder: my notebook. I check it against my calls each morning. Each line shows when the text went, the job number, the phone and the code:
Soon after, Ms Tremellen rang back from her doorstep. Her key safe wouldn't open. 9026 is not her code. It opens a box on a stranger's door across town.
The text went to the right phone. The code belonged to another door.

Teodric drove out and opened her lock by hand. Nobody went near Haverick Close, and Mr Dunwiddie's code was changed by morning. Grisell says nobody could have typed 9026 into Ms Tremellen's job, and Node never does two things at once. What should she change before tonight?

blocks.label: notebook_0247_redrawn.png
blocks.caption: Grisell redrew my four notebook lines from 02:47:31 as a sequence, read top to bottom. Each request sets current.job and asks the geocoder where its street is. Job 2414 sets current.job at .200, while job 2413 is still waiting. At .300 job 2413 gets its answer and reads the code from current.job. At .500 job 2414 does the same. Both texts carry 9026.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Grisell's tidy-up has a name. Programmers keep a catalogue of design patterns: named shapes of code for problems that keep coming back, each with places it fits and places it doesn't. The singleton is one of them. Now read your notebook next to her five lines of code. For each moment from 02:47:31.000 to .500, write down what current.job held and which request had put it there. Then find the one line that builds the text. Where does it take the phone number from, and where the code? And ask Grisell what else in the app reaches into that object.

replies.author: u/night_dispatch_vasilisa
replies.text: Grisell says the singleton came from a 1994 book of patterns, and the app uses two more. A factory: one place that builds the right kind of job, house, car or safe, from what I type. And an observer: the van's tablet signs up to be told whenever a job is booked. The singleton also holds our settings, the values that are the same for every call-out: the text company's web address and the night rate.

comments.author: u/single_thread_eberhard
comments.text: Node has one thread. It runs one piece of code at a time, start to finish, so two requests can't be inside dispatch together and can't trample each other. This is impossible in Node. Somebody typed the wrong code by hand, or pasted it from the last job. My advice: log the singleton's job number before every text. Then the morning's check of your notebook proves who sent what, and you can stop blaming the code.

replies.author: u/night_dispatch_vasilisa
replies.text: Nobody typed Mr Dunwiddie's job. He booked it on the website at 02:47:31.200, and I was still typing Ms Tremellen's address into the notes.

comments.author: u/clean_slate_morwick
comments.text: Leftovers are the classic bug. Whatever the last call-out put in current.job is still sitting there when the next one starts. Clear it after each text is sent, and every call-out starts from empty.

replies.author: u/night_dispatch_vasilisa
replies.text: Teodric would rather put the call-outs in a queue: a line where each one waits its turn and runs start to finish before the next begins. He says nobody minds waiting a third of a second.

reply.prompt: Call-outs will come in close together again tonight. What should Grisell change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Queue call-outs so the app handles one at a time, start to finish, before the next begins.
options.part2: Grisell put the call-outs in a line. A week later two came in 200 ms apart again. The second waited in line from .200 until the first had sent its text at .300, then asked the geocoder and texted its own code at .600, a wait of 400 ms instead of 300. Both codes were right. Then the geocoder had a slow night and took 2,000 ms an answer: the second caller's text waited 3,800 ms, and on a busy night every caller waits for everyone ahead. And current.job is still there. Last week Grisell added a price check that runs outside the line, and the first thing it does is read current.job.
options.senior: A queue removes the overlap, so the shared object can't be overwritten mid-request, and the codes come out right. But it buys safety by giving up the very thing Node is good at: getting on with other work while one request waits. Every call-out now waits behind every geocoder answer ahead of it. And the cause, request data in a global, is still in the code for the next helper that doesn't go through the queue.

options.text: Clear the current job after each text is sent, so the next call-out always starts from empty.
options.verdict: Clears it at the wrong moment
options.part2: Grisell added one line: after each text, current.job is emptied. A week later two call-outs came in 200 ms apart. The first saved its job at .000; the second overwrote it at .200; at .300 the first woke and texted its own customer the second customer's code, exactly as before, and then cleared current.job. At .500 the second woke, found current.job empty, and the code failed with an error. No text went at all. One customer had a stranger's code and the other had nothing, and I only knew when both rang.
options.senior: Clearing deals with leftovers between call-outs, but the mix happens during one: the second request writes while the first is paused at await. Clearing after the text comes too late for the first caller and too early for the second, so it keeps the leak and adds a crash. Any fix that still keeps one request's data in a shared place depends on timing, and timing is exactly what a busy night changes.

options.text: Pass each call-out's job to every function that needs it; keep the singleton for settings.
options.part2: Grisell changed one line to sms(job.phone, job.keySafe) and took the job out of the shared object altogether, so nothing can reach for it. The singleton now holds only the settings: the text company's address and the night rate. Each paused dispatch keeps its own job, and nothing another request does can touch it. A week later two call-outs came in 200 ms apart. The first texted its own code at .300, the second its own at .500, with no waiting in line. For her new log helper, which twelve functions call, she wrapped each request in AsyncLocalStorage so the helper can ask for that request's own job. My notebook has matched my calls every morning since.
options.senior: Data that belongs to one request travels with that request: as a parameter, or in a per-request context where passing it is impractical. Then an await is harmless, because the paused function holds its own job and no other request can reach it. The singleton keeps the job it is fit for, settings that are the same for everyone. Patterns are tools with a fit; a singleton holding request data is a global variable with a nicer name.

options.text: Log the singleton's job number before each text, so a mix-up shows in the morning's check.
options.verdict: Finds it after the door is open
options.part2: Grisell added the log line. A week later two call-outs came in 200 ms apart, and at .300 the first customer was texted the second customer's code, exactly as before. This time the notebook said why: job 2414's number on job 2413's phone. My morning check found it hours after a stranger had been given the code to someone's front door. Nobody used it, as far as we know. The code was changed again.
options.senior: Logging is detection, and detection after the fact is the wrong tool for a mistake that does its harm the moment it happens. Here, the harm is a door code on the wrong phone. The log helps you prove what went wrong, which matters, but it changes nothing about why: one request's data sits where every other request can overwrite it. Fix the cause first, then keep the log as the alarm for the next one.

sim.title: Replay the night's call-outs
sim.lede: You're Grisell, replaying the night from 22:58:00, before the first call-out. Six call-outs come in; 2413 and 2414 arrive 200 ms apart at 02:47:31. Each runs dispatch(job): it saves the job in current.job, the singleton, waits for the geocoder (300 ms), then texts its phone the code it finds in current.job at that moment. Sending the text is counted as instant. Node takes one step at a time; when a geocoder answer and a new call-out land in the same millisecond, the answer goes first. Change the gap, the geocoder's delay and the design: the singleton as built, a queue that runs one call-out at a time, clearing current.job after each text, logging current.job's number before each text, or passing the job. The pattern picker shows where each of six patterns fits.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step seven times and watch current.job change hands at 02:47:31.200, then job 2413 text 9026 at .300. Play the rest. Set the gap to 300 ms, then 0. Set the geocoder to 2,000 ms. Try the queue and read Mr Dunwiddie's time, then clear-after, then the log. Last, pass the job, at a gap of 0 and a 2,000 ms geocoder.

explain.oneLine: Nobody typed the wrong code. Both call-outs shared one current job, and while the first waited 300 ms for the geocoder the second overwrote it, so the first texted its own customer's phone with the second customer's code.

steps.title: One object, every request.
steps.text: Grisell's tidy-up made one object, current, when the app starts, and every call-out uses that same object. A function that wants the job no longer gets it handed in; it reaches into current.job. Inside one request that works exactly as before. The difference only shows when two requests are alive at once, because there is still only one current.job for both of them to write into.

steps.title: await lets the second call-out in.
steps.text: First, at 02:47:31.000, dispatch for job 2413 saved its job in current.job. Second, it reached await geocode and paused, and Node's event loop, its one thread working through a to-do list, went on to other work. Third, at .200, job 2414 arrived, and its dispatch saved its own job in the same current.job, overwriting job 2413's while it slept. Fourth, at .300, the geocoder answered job 2413 and its dispatch carried on: it took the phone from its own job and the code from current.job, which now held job 2414. Last, at .500, job 2414 woke and texted its own code, correctly. Node never ran two lines at once; it switched requests at each await, and that was enough. Any call-out arriving inside another's 300 ms wait does this.

steps.title: A singleton is a global variable with a nicer name.
steps.text: A global variable is a value any part of the program can read and change. Design Patterns gives the singleton's aim as one instance with a global point of access, and that is exactly the danger: whatever one request writes there, every other request reads. For settings that are the same for everyone, such as the text company's address, that is useful. For anything that belongs to one call-out, it is memory shared between strangers, and the tidy name hides it. It is the same family of bug as a race condition between threads (s5e01), but here there is one thread and the gap is every await.

steps.title: Patterns are named shapes, each with a fit.
steps.text: A design pattern is a known shape of code for a problem that keeps coming back. Strategy puts several ways of doing one job behind the same call, so pricing can use the day rate or the night rate without an if in every function. A factory is one place that decides which kind of object to make, such as a house, car or safe job. An observer lets other parts sign up to be told when something happens, like the van's tablet hearing about a new job. An adapter wraps someone else's code, such as the text company's service, so it looks like the sms() your code expects. A decorator wraps an object to add a duty, such as a retry, without changing it. A singleton gives the whole program one shared instance. Each fits a problem, and each, misused, adds one; the singleton's misuse is the quietest.

steps.title: Keep each call-out's data with the call-out.
steps.text: First, hand the job to every function that needs it, as a parameter: sms(job.phone, job.keySafe). Each paused dispatch then keeps its own job, and nothing another request does can change it. Second, take the job out of the shared object, so no helper can reach for it by habit. Third, where a value is needed deep inside many helpers, such as the job number for a log line, use Node's per-request store, AsyncLocalStorage: wrap the request once in als.run(job, ...), and any helper inside calls als.getStore() to get that request's job back, even after an await. What can go wrong: a helper called outside run() gets undefined, so check for it.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tonight. Call-out 2413, code 3158, hands its own job to dispatch, which texts 3158 at .300. Call-out 2414, code 9026, hands its own job to a second dispatch, which texts 9026 at .500. A settings singleton on the right holds the text company's address and the night rate; both dispatches read it, and it holds no call-out.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tonight. Each call-out hands its own job to its own dispatch, so the code in the text comes from the same job as the phone. The singleton still exists, but it holds only what every call-out shares: the text company's address and the night rate. A second call-out arriving 200 ms later has nothing of the first's to overwrite.

fix.title: The fix: pass the job; keep the singleton for settings
fix.text: Change dispatch so every function gets the call-out it is working on: geocode(job.address), then sms(job.phone, job.keySafe). Take the job out of the shared object entirely, so no helper can reach for it, and leave only settings there: the text company's address and the night rate, the same for every call-out. Where a value must reach deep helpers without being passed through every call, use AsyncLocalStorage: one run(job, ...) at the start of the request, and getStore() where it's needed. Then search the code for every other place that reads current, and fix each one the same way.

limits: Passing the job only protects code that uses the passed job. A helper that still reads a shared object, or a new one written next month, brings the mix back, so review for module-level objects that hold one request's data.
AsyncLocalStorage keeps the right job across await, but only inside the run() that set it. Work started outside it gets undefined, so check that getStore() actually returns a job before using it.

Passing the job makes every function's list of inputs longer, and deep chains carry a value only the bottom needs. AsyncLocalStorage helps there, at the cost of a hidden input that is easy to forget is there.

explain.seniorTake: Patterns are vocabulary, not virtue: each names a shape and the problem it fits, and each one used outside its fit causes the trouble it was meant to avoid. Question the singleton first, because it is a global variable with a respectable name. In a server that handles many requests, ask of every shared object: does this belong to everyone, or to one request? Settings can be shared. A user, a tenant, a job or a basket cannot. One thread doesn't save you, because every await is a gap where another request runs. Pass request data in, use a per-request context such as AsyncLocalStorage where passing is impractical, and treat any module-level value that changes per request as a bug waiting for a busy night.

realWorld.title: Design Patterns, 1994: the singleton's intent
realWorld.text: A pattern catalogue that credits Design Patterns (Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides) gives the singleton's intent as "Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it". The global point of access is the feature, and it is what turns one request's data into data every request shares.

realWorld.title: The book and its four authors
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article on Design Patterns says "The book was written by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides" and that it "was originally published on 21 October 1994, with a 1995 copyright". It cites the book for "Program to an interface, not an implementation."

realWorld.title: The usual criticism: global state
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article on the singleton pattern: "Some consider the singleton to be an anti-pattern that introduces global state into an application, often unnecessarily."

realWorld.title: Strategy: interchangeable ways to do one job
realWorld.text: The catalogue's strategy entry gives the intent as "Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable." And: "Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it." Day, night and trade rates are a family like that.

realWorld.title: Factory Method: one place decides what to make
realWorld.text: The factory method entry: "Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate." And: "Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses."

realWorld.title: Decorator: add a duty without changing the object
realWorld.text: The decorator entry: "Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically." And: "Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality". A retry wrapped around sending a text is one.

realWorld.title: Observer, as the catalogue words it
realWorld.text: The catalogue states observer's intent in its own words: "An observer defines a dependency relationship between objects so that, when the state of an object changes, all its dependents are automatically notified and updated."

realWorld.title: Adapter, as the catalogue words it
realWorld.text: And adapter's: "An adapter converts the interface from one class to another in accordance with the client's expectations." The text company's service wrapped to look like sms() is that.

realWorld.title: Node.js: a store per request
realWorld.text: The Node.js documentation says AsyncLocalStorage "creates stores that stay coherent through asynchronous operations." Of run(): "The store is accessible to any asynchronous operations created within the callback." getStore() "Returns the current store", and returns undefined outside one. It adds that AsyncLocalStorage "should be preferred as it is a performant and memory safe implementation".

asked: Name three design patterns and when you'd use them.
How do you keep per-request state in Node?
interview.answer: A singleton is one shared instance with a global point of access, so it is global state with a nicer name. That is fine for things that are truly the same for everyone, such as settings, but it hides dependencies, makes tests share state, and in a server it becomes a leak the moment it holds one request's data: another request overwrites it. Three patterns: strategy, when you have interchangeable ways to do one job, such as pricing rules, and want to pick one per call without if-chains; factory, when one place should decide which concrete class to create from some input; observer, when several parts need to react to an event without the source knowing who they are. Adapter and decorator are worth naming too: wrap a third-party interface to fit yours, or wrap an object to add a duty such as retries or logging. Per-request state in Node: Node runs every request on one thread, but each await lets other requests run in between, so module-level variables are shared across requests that are in flight at once. Pass request data as parameters. Where it must reach deep helpers, such as a request id for logging, use AsyncLocalStorage: run(store, fn) at the start of the request and getStore() wherever it's needed, which stays correct across await.

atWork: Look for a current user or current tenant kept in a module-level object in a web service: a value at the top of a file, set at the start of each request so helpers can reach it. It is a common pattern, and it is safe only if nothing between setting it and reading it ever waits. Read-only access to the code is enough to check. Search for module-level objects or variables that are assigned inside a request handler, then look for any await between that assignment and a later read. Each one is a place where one customer's data can end up in another customer's answer. Replace it with a parameter, or in Node with AsyncLocalStorage. If you handle EU residents' personal data, GDPR Art. 32(1)(b) asks for measures that ensure "the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services"; one customer's door code on another's phone is a confidentiality failure. If your company is pursuing SOC 2, criterion CC6.1, on logical access, applies too: a request should reach only its own customer's data. Build the rule in now, no request data in shared objects and a check for it in review, rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's online shop runs on Node. A module-level object, currentUser, is set at the start of each request so helpers can reach it. Between setting it and building the order confirmation, the code awaits a database call. Under load, one customer's confirmation shows another customer's delivery address. What is happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: currentUser is global state: a second request overwrites it while the first is paused at await
One thread doesn't prevent it, because every await lets other requests run in between
Pass the user as a parameter, or keep it in a per-request context such as AsyncLocalStorage

recall.model: currentUser is global state with a nicer name: one object shared by every request. Request A sets it to its customer and pauses at the database await. Node, which runs on one thread, uses that pause to start request B, which overwrites currentUser with its own customer. When A wakes, it builds its confirmation from B's user. Being single-threaded doesn't prevent it, because every await lets other requests run in between. Pass the user to each function as a parameter, or keep it in a per-request context such as AsyncLocalStorage, and leave the module-level object for settings that are the same for everyone.

recall.prompt: dispatch sets current.job, then awaits a geocoder that takes 300 ms, then reads current.job.keySafe for the text. A second call-out arrives some time after the first. When does the first caller get the second caller's code?
options: Only when both arrive in the same millisecond
Whenever the second arrives less than 300 ms after the first
Whenever the second arrives more than 300 ms after the first
Never, because Node runs one request at a time
recall.why: The first call-out reads current.job when the geocoder answers, 300 ms after it set it. Any call-out that arrives inside that window overwrites current.job first. At 300 ms or later, the first has already sent its text. Node runs one step at a time, but it switches between requests at every await.

recall.prompt: Grisell has three jobs for the app: (a) price a call-out at the day, night or trade rate, chosen per call-out; (b) make the text company's service, which wants sendMessage(to, body), fit the sms(phone, code) her code calls; (c) tell the van's tablet and the notebook whenever a job is booked. Name a design pattern for each, and say what, if anything, still belongs in the singleton.

keyIdeas.idea: Strategy for the rates: interchangeable pricing objects behind one call
Adapter for the text company: a wrapper that fits their interface to sms()
Observer for bookings: the tablet and notebook subscribe and are notified
The singleton keeps only settings that are the same for every call-out

recall.model: (a) Strategy: each rate is its own small pricing object behind the same price(job) call, and each call-out picks one, so a new rate is a new object, not a new if in every function. (b) Adapter: a thin wrapper with sms(phone, code) that calls the company's sendMessage(to, body) underneath, so the rest of the code never sees their interface. (c) Observer: the tablet and the notebook subscribe to a job-booked event and are notified each time, so booking doesn't need to know who is listening. The singleton should hold only settings that are the same for every call-out, such as the text company's address and the rate table, and nothing that belongs to one job.

recall.prompt: Which of these is safe to keep in a singleton in a Node server that handles many requests at once?
options: The signed-in user for the request being handled
The text company's web address and the night rate
The job the current request is working on
The customer's phone number for the text being sent
recall.why: Only the settings are the same for every request, so sharing them can't mix anything up. The user, the job and the phone number each belong to one request; in a shared object, another request can overwrite them while the first is paused at an await.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Every function now takes its job, and not one wrong code since. Last week Grisell added a log helper that twelve functions call. Rather than pass the job through all twelve, the helper reads a module-level variable, logJobId, which dispatch sets as its first line. On Tuesday at 01:40 two call-outs came in 100 ms apart. Both customers got their own codes. But my notebook says "text sent" twice for job 2588 and never for job 2587.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the notebook name the wrong job when every code was right, and how should the log helper get the job number without it going through twelve functions?

keyIdeas.idea: logJobId is shared state again: the second dispatch overwrote it while the first was paused at an await
The codes are right because they come from the job each function was handed; only the log reads shared data
Use AsyncLocalStorage: run(job, ...) in dispatch, getStore() in the log helper

coldCase.model: It's the same bug in a smaller place. logJobId is one variable shared by every call-out. Job 2587's dispatch set it, then paused at the geocoder's await; 100 ms later job 2588's dispatch overwrote it, so when 2587 logged its text, the helper read 2588. The codes were right because sms() now uses the job each function was handed as a parameter; only the log helper still reads shared data. Don't go back to a global. Wrap each dispatch in AsyncLocalStorage, als.run(job, () => dispatch(job)), and in the log helper call als.getStore() to get that request's own job, even after an await. Nothing has to go through the twelve functions, and no other request can change it.
